venues.name: The Balmoral, a Rocco Forte Hotel
venues.area: New Town / Old Town line, 1 Princes Street, above Waverley
venues.note: The city's landmark grand hotel beneath its famous clock tower, Rocco Forte's Edinburgh flagship, and the first hotel in Scotland to earn Forbes Five Stars.

venues.name: Gleneagles Townhouse
venues.note: The city outpost of Scotland's iconic Gleneagles estate, a former bank on St Andrew Square, part hotel, part members' club, with a glass-domed dining room.

venues.name: 100 Princes Street
venues.area: New Town, 100 Princes Street, facing the Castle
venues.note: An intimate 30-room house on Princes Street from Red Carnation, in the former home of a Scottish explorers' club, two staff to every guest, and full-on castle views.

venues.name: Prestonfield House
venues.area: Newington, under Arthur's Seat, 10 minutes from the centre
venues.note: A theatrical 17th-century mansion in 20 acres of parkland with peacocks on the lawn, the most opulent, romantic country house within the city bounds.

venues.name: The Witchery by the Castle
venues.area: Old Town, Castlehill, at the gates of Edinburgh Castle
venues.note: Nine gothic, theatrical suites in 16th-century buildings at the very top of the Royal Mile, the most singular, atmospheric stay in Edinburgh.

venues.name: Waldorf Astoria Edinburgh, The Caledonian
venues.area: West End, Princes Street, by the Castle
venues.note: The grand former railway hotel at the west end of Princes Street, a Victorian landmark of red sandstone with a great spa and Castle views.

venues.name: Kimpton Charlotte Square
venues.area: New Town, Charlotte Square, West End
venues.note: Seven Georgian townhouses on the New Town's most elegant square, wrapped around a glass-roofed courtyard garden, polished, warm and unstuffy.

venues.name: The Glasshouse, Autograph Collection
venues.note: A design hotel behind a preserved 1846 church façade, crowned by a two-acre rooftop garden with views to Calton Hill and the Firth.

venues.name: W Edinburgh
venues.area: St James Quarter, Calton Hill edge
venues.note: Scotland's first W, a bold, high-design hotel in the St James Quarter with a rooftop bar and 'ribbon' architecture, for members who want the new and the loud.

venues.name: Restaurant Martin Wishart
venues.note: Scotland's longest-held Michelin star, refined modern French cooking on the Leith waterfront, a star for a quarter of a century.

venues.name: The Kitchin
venues.note: Tom Kitchin's 'from nature to plate' cooking on the Leith shore, Scottish seasonal produce and French technique, starred since 2007.

venues.name: Condita
venues.note: A candle-lit, six-table room doing a single no-choice tasting menu, the city's most intimate and personal Michelin experience.

venues.name: Heron
venues.area: Leith, Bonnington Road, on the Water of Leith
venues.note: Tomás Gormley and Sam Yorke's calm canal-side room, precise, produce-led tasting menus that won a star and hold it.

venues.name: Timberyard
venues.area: Old Town, Lady Lawson Street, near the Castle
venues.note: A family-run former timber warehouse doing wild, foraged, live-fire Scottish cooking, a Michelin star and, latterly, a Green Star for its sustainability.

venues.name: Lyla
venues.area: New Town, Royal Terrace, Calton Hill
venues.note: Stuart Ralston's seafood-focused tasting-menu room on Royal Terrace, a 'nature to plate' journey through Scottish produce, starred in 2025.

venues.name: Avery
venues.note: Rodney Wages moved his restaurant from San Francisco to a Stockbridge townhouse, a 15-course tasting menu that earned a star within a year of opening.

venues.name: Skua
venues.note: A relaxed Leith seafood spot from the Heron team, Scottish coastal ingredients served simply, and a Michelin Bib Gourmand for it.

venues.name: Noto
venues.note: Stuart Ralston's relaxed New Town room, Japanese-influenced small plates on Scottish produce, a long-standing Bib Gourmand.

venues.name: The Scran & Scallie
venues.note: Tom Kitchin's laid-back gastropub in Stockbridge, proper Scottish comfort cooking with a Bib Gourmand and a fireside welcome.

venues.name: Ardfern
venues.note: A tiny Leith restaurant with a weekly-changing menu built around the best of Scottish farms and waters, a Bib Gourmand for honest, seasonal cooking.

venues.name: Aizle
venues.area: New Town, The Kimpton Charlotte Square
venues.note: Stuart Ralston's original Edinburgh restaurant, a surprise seasonal tasting menu now set within Kimpton Charlotte Square, a MICHELIN Guide room.

venues.name: Fhior
venues.note: Scott and Laura Smith's ingredient-driven room on Broughton Street, nature-led Scottish tasting menus, listed in the MICHELIN Guide.

venues.name: The Little Chartroom
venues.note: Roberta Hall-McCarron's much-loved bistro, precise, seasonal small-plate and set-menu cooking, a fixture of the MICHELIN Guide.

venues.name: Edinburgh Castle
venues.note: The fortress on the black volcanic rock is the city's beating heart, crown jewels, the Stone of Destiny, and the one-o'clock gun fired daily since 1861. A private early-access or after-hours guide lets a multi-generation family have the Great Hall and battlements almost to themselves before the crowds and the coaches arrive.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old and New Towns of Edinburgh

venues.name: The Royal Mile
venues.note: The mile-long spine of the Old Town runs downhill from the Castle to Holyrood, past closes, kirks, tartan windows and the High Kirk of St Giles. Walk it with a storyteller-guide who peels back the wynds and hidden courtyards the guidebook crowds stream straight past.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old and New Towns of Edinburgh

venues.name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
venues.note: The King's official residence in Scotland, at the foot of the Royal Mile, Mary, Queen of Scots' chambers, the ruined abbey, and state apartments still used for royal ceremony. A quiet, richly historic counterpoint to the Castle, and rarely rushed.

venues.name: Arthur's Seat & Holyrood Park
venues.note: An extinct volcano rising 251 metres straight out of the city, ringed by a royal park of crags, lochs and grazing land. The summit gives the finest panorama of Edinburgh; a private guide can pick the gentler Dunsapie approach so grandparents and grandchildren reach the top together.

venues.name: Calton Hill
venues.note: The easy-to-reach hill crowned with the half-finished National Monument, the Nelson Monument and the Dugald Stewart Monument, the postcard view of the city and the Firth of Forth. Golden hour here is the single best photograph you'll take in Edinburgh.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old and New Towns of Edinburgh

venues.name: National Museum of Scotland
venues.note: A soaring Victorian glasshouse joined to a modern gallery, holding everything from Dolly the cloned sheep to Lewis chessmen and Scottish design. Free, vast and genuinely all-ages, the roof terrace view is a quiet local secret, and there's easy veg-friendly dining in the grand hall.

venues.name: Scottish National Gallery
venues.note: The nation's great collection sits between the two halves of Princes Street Gardens, Titian, Vermeer, Raeburn's skating minister, and a superb room of Scottish colourists. Compact enough for an unhurried hour with a private art guide before lunch.

venues.name: Scottish National Portrait Gallery
venues.note: A red-sandstone neo-Gothic palace on Queen Street, its arcaded entrance hall a frieze of Scottish history, its rooms full of the faces that made the nation, from Mary, Queen of Scots to Sean Connery. Beautiful, calm and free.

venues.name: New Town & the Georgian House
venues.note: The 18th-century planned New Town, Charlotte Square, Georgian terraces, ordered elegance that reshaped European city-building. The restored Georgian House on the square shows exactly how the merchant aristocracy lived; a walking guide reads the whole ensemble.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old and New Towns of Edinburgh

venues.name: Princes Street Gardens
venues.note: The green valley below the Castle, where a railway once was and a loch before that, lawns, the Ross Fountain, and the finest ground-level view of the Old Town skyline. An easy, restful pause between shopping and sightseeing.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old and New Towns of Edinburgh

venues.name: The Scott Monument
venues.note: The soaring Gothic rocket built to honour Sir Walter Scott, the largest monument to a writer in the world, with a marble statue of the author at its base. The fit can climb its 287 narrow steps for a caged panorama; the view from the gardens below is glorious without the climb.
credentials: Largest monument to a writer in the world

venues.name: Dean Village & the Water of Leith
venues.note: A hidden former milling hamlet of Tudor-esque buildings tucked in a river gorge minutes from Princes Street, improbably picturesque and blissfully quiet. Follow the Water of Leith walkway past St Bernard's Well; a photographer's and stroller's delight.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old and New Towns of Edinburgh

venues.name: Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh
venues.note: Seventy acres of one of the world's great botanic gardens, Victorian glasshouses, a Chinese hillside, the largest cultivated collection of rhododendrons anywhere, and a skyline view back to the city. Peaceful, pram-friendly, and lovely for three generations at an easy pace.
credentials: One of the world's leading botanic gardens

venues.name: Camera Obscura & World of Illusions
venues.note: A Victorian 'camera obscura' at the top of the Royal Mile that projects a live moving image of the city onto a dish, plus five floors of mirror mazes and optical trickery. A guaranteed winner with children and the young-at-heart, and the rooftop gives a free Castle view.

venues.name: The Real Mary King's Close
venues.note: A warren of genuine 17th-century streets and homes sealed and buried beneath the Royal Mile, now brought alive by costumed character-guides. Atmospheric, a little spooky, and unlike anything else in the city, best booked as a private timed tour.

venues.name: Greyfriars Kirkyard
venues.note: The evocative old graveyard behind the National Museum, resting place of city grandees, birthplace of the loyal-dog legend Greyfriars Bobby, and, some say, the source of names J.K. Rowling borrowed for Harry Potter. A gentle, literary detour.

venues.name: The Writers' Museum
venues.note: A tucked-away 17th-century townhouse in Lady Stair's Close devoted to Scotland's literary giants, Robert Burns, Sir Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson. Small, free, and a fitting stop in the world's first UNESCO City of Literature.

venues.name: St Giles' Cathedral
venues.note: The great High Kirk on the Royal Mile, its crown-shaped spire a city landmark, inside, the jewel-like Thistle Chapel with its intricately carved stalls is one of Scotland's finest interiors. A guided visit reads the stained glass and 900 years of turbulent history.

venues.name: Victoria Street
venues.note: The curving, rainbow-fronted Old Town street of independent shops widely thought to have inspired Harry Potter's Diagon Alley. Photogenic from the Bow above and full of small pleasures, a bookseller of magic, a cheesemonger, a joke shop, for a leisurely browse.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Old and New Towns of Edinburgh

venues.name: Grassmarket
venues.note: A wide, cobbled square in the Castle's shadow that was once a livestock market and place of execution, now lined with pubs, boutiques and independent shops. A lively spot for people-watching with the fortress rearing above you.

venues.name: Stockbridge
venues.note: The village-within-the-city, a genteel neighbourhood of independent delis, antique shops and the colonnaded Sunday market, beside the Water of Leith. A refined, unhurried morning away from the tourist track, with strong cafe and veg-friendly dining options.

venues.name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
venues.note: Right beside the Castle, an introduction to Scotland's regions and distilling, home to the world's largest collection of Scotch whisky, nearly 3,500 bottles. The tasting tours suit both a first-timer and a connoisseur, and the shop can source rarities.
credentials: Home to the world's largest collection of Scotch whisky

venues.name: Johnnie Walker Princes Street
venues.note: Eight floors of interactive whisky storytelling in a landmarked Art Deco former department store, topped by the 1820 rooftop bars looking straight across to the Castle. Personalised tastings and a superb rooftop cocktail-and-view finish make it a polished flagship experience.

venues.name: The Royal Yacht Britannia
venues.note: The late Queen's floating royal home for over 40 years, berthed at Leith, five decks of state apartments, the royal bedrooms and the Rolls-Royce garage, all frozen as they were. Repeatedly rated among the world's very best attractions; end with tea and cake in the Royal Deck Tea Room.
credentials: Repeatedly rated Tripadvisor's No.1 Attraction in the World

venues.name: Leith & The Shore
venues.note: Edinburgh's revitalised historic port, cobbled quaysides, converted warehouses and the city's densest cluster of fine dining, including its Michelin-starred kitchens. Arrive by the modern tram and make an evening of it on the waterfront.

venues.name: Dynamic Earth
venues.note: An immersive science attraction beneath Arthur's Seat that travels from the Big Bang through ice ages to the present, with a full-dome planetarium. The most engaging rainy-day option for families with curious children.

venues.name: Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art (Modern One & Two)
venues.note: Two neoclassical buildings in landscaped grounds, a Charles Jencks landform, a Paolozzi studio recreation, and Dada and Surrealist treasures. A calm, cultured half-day reached along the Water of Leith, and free to enter.

venues.name: Museum of Edinburgh & the Canongate
venues.note: In the lower, quieter reach of the Royal Mile, a rambling 16th-century townhouse telling the story of the city itself, near the handsome Canongate Kirk. A pleasant, low-key stop between the Palace and the Parliament.

venues.name: Scottish Parliament
venues.note: Enric Miralles' bold, controversial 2004 building at the foot of the Royal Mile, a much-awarded piece of modern architecture that rewards a guided tour of its debating chamber and inventive detail. A striking contrast to the ancient stone all around it.

venues.name: The Meadows & Bruntsfield Links
venues.note: A broad, tree-lined common south of the Old Town, framed by the cherry-blossom avenue that draws the whole city each spring. An easy, green stroll where local Edinburgh unwinds, well away from the crowds.

venues.name: Victoria Terrace & the Vennel viewpoint
venues.note: Two of the city's best free photographs, the balcony walkway above Victoria Street, and the stepped Vennel closes off the Grassmarket that frame the Castle perfectly between old tenement walls. A guide who knows the light will time them for you.

venues.name: Blackford Hill & the Royal Observatory
venues.note: A quiet suburban hill giving a full panorama over the city to the Castle and the Forth, crowned by the Victorian Royal Observatory. A local's viewpoint, easily worked into a private half-day by car.

venues.name: Craigmillar Castle
venues.note: One of Scotland's best-preserved medieval castles, where Mary, Queen of Scots once sheltered, dramatic, atmospheric and, remarkably for its quality, almost tourist-free. A rewarding short drive for those who want history without the queues.

venues.name: Edinburgh International Festival & the Fringe
venues.note: Every August the whole city becomes a stage, the International Festival's world-class opera, theatre and orchestras alongside the Fringe, the largest arts festival on earth. Book premium tickets and a hotel far in advance; a concierge is close to essential in peak season.

venues.name: The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo
venues.note: Massed pipes and drums and international performers on the Castle esplanade each August, floodlit against the ramparts, one of the great spectacles in the world calendar. Reserved premium seating and a private car for the departure crush make the night effortless.

venues.name: Edinburgh's Christmas & Hogmanay
venues.note: The winter city glows, a Christmas market and rink in Princes Street Gardens, and the world-famous three-day Hogmanay street party and fireworks over the Castle. Hospitality packages and a guide turn a heaving crowd into a warm, easy celebration.
credentials: One of the world's most famous New Year celebrations

venues.name: Rosslyn Chapel
venues.note: Seven miles south, the astonishingly carved 15th-century chapel of 'The Da Vinci Code' fame, every surface a riot of angels, greenery and enigmatic symbols. Small, richly atmospheric, and best reached by private car with a guide who can decode the stonework.

venues.name: Stirling Castle
venues.note: Under an hour away, one of Scotland's grandest and most important castles, magnificently sited on its crag with the restored golden-stone Renaissance palace of the Stuart kings. Pair it with the nearby Wallace Monument and the Kelpies for a full, cinematic day out.

venues.name: The Forth Bridges & South Queensferry
venues.note: Just west of the city, the mighty red cantilever Forth Bridge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, spans the firth beside its two road bridges. Lunch in pretty South Queensferry and take a cruise out to Inchcolm Abbey for the best perspective of all three.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, The Forth Bridge

venues.name: Glasgow
venues.note: Under an hour by train or car, Scotland's confident second city, the free Kelvingrove and Burrell Collection, Charles Rennie Mackintosh's architecture, and the country's best shopping and dining. A vivid, characterful contrast to genteel Edinburgh.

venues.name: The Highlands, Glencoe & the West
venues.note: For those with a full day and a chauffeur, the road north opens onto Rannoch Moor and the brooding grandeur of Glencoe, arguably Scotland's most dramatic glen, with the Glenfinnan viaduct and Loch Ness within reach on longer runs. Best done privately, at your own pace.

venues.name: The Kelpies & Falkirk Wheel
venues.note: Half an hour west, two feats of engineering-as-art, Andy Scott's 30-metre steel horse-heads, the largest equine sculptures in the world, and the only rotating boat lift on earth. A short, memorable stop that delights children and design lovers alike.
credentials: The Kelpies, world's largest equine sculptures
Falkirk Wheel, world's only rotating boat lift

venues.name: North Berwick & the Scottish Seabird Centre
venues.note: A genteel seaside town under 40 minutes east, with golden beaches, a five-star wildlife centre and boat trips to the Bass Rock, the world's largest colony of Northern gannets. A breezy, family-friendly counterpoint to the city, with fine golf on the coast.
credentials: Bass Rock, world's largest Northern gannet colony

venues.name: Panda & Sons
venues.note: Hidden behind a mock barber-shop front, Iain McPherson's speakeasy is the highest-ranked bar in Scotland, and No.1 in the world's Top 500 for 2025.
credentials: No. 1 in the World's 50 Best Bars Top 500 (2025)

venues.name: Bramble
venues.note: A basement bar under a dry cleaner's that helped define modern cocktails in Britain, low-lit, intimate and consistently world-ranked.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery

venues.name: Nauticus
venues.note: An ocean-themed Leith bar from the Panda & Sons team, championing Scottish spirits and produce, a shore-town local with world-class drinks.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery

venues.name: The Last Word Saloon
venues.note: A cosy, wood-panelled saloon in Stockbridge from the Bramble team, vintage feel, expert classics and the eponymous Last Word done properly.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery

venues.name: The Lucky Liquor Co.
venues.note: A tiny, playful bar built on the number 13, thirteen spirits, thirteen drinks, changing every thirteen weeks, from the Bramble family.
credentials: The World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery

venues.name: The Lamplighters
venues.area: New Town, Gleneagles Townhouse, St Andrew Square
venues.note: The clubby cocktail bar of Gleneagles Townhouse, a glamorous, low-lit room under the dome of a former bank, one of the city's most stylish drinks addresses.
credentials: Inside Gleneagles Townhouse, a MICHELIN One-Key hotel

venues.name: SCOTCH at The Balmoral
venues.area: New Town, The Balmoral, Princes Street
venues.note: A wood-panelled whisky bar in the Balmoral with more than 500 malts and a resident whisky ambassador, the finest place in town to explore Scotch.
credentials: Inside The Balmoral, a Forbes Five-Star, MICHELIN Two-Key hotel
